epithet.en: Greatest of the Greek warriors, son of Peleus and the goddess Thetis, whose wrath drives the entire poem

1.modern-en: Achilles quarrels with Agamemnon over the captive Briseis; when Agamemnon takes her by force, Achilles withdraws from battle in furious wrath and asks his mother Thetis to petition Zeus to punish the Greeks.

2.modern-en: Achilles remains absent from the assembly and the marshaling of troops—his name is spoken by others but he takes no part as the Achaeans prepare for battle without him.

3.modern-en: Achilles is absent from the truce and the single combat between Paris and Menelaus, still nursing his anger at the ships.

4.modern-en: Apollo reminds the Trojans that Achilles is not fighting; his absence is felt as the real reason the Greeks are vulnerable.

5.modern-en: Achilles is still absent; Diomedes fills the warrior vacuum in his place, performing the great feats of this book.

6.modern-en: Achilles does not appear; the Trojans and Greeks fight on the plain without him.

7.modern-en: Achilles remains withdrawn; Hector and Ajax duel while Achilles watches from afar.

8.modern-en: Achilles is still absent as Zeus tips the battle toward the Trojans and drives the Greeks back to their wall.

9.modern-en: Agamemnon sends Phoenix, Odysseus, and Ajax to beg Achilles to return, offering vast gifts and Briseis back. Achilles refuses, saying he will sail home at dawn—though he ultimately does not leave.

10.modern-en: Achilles does not appear in the night raid; Odysseus and Diomedes carry out the mission without him.

11.modern-en: Achilles watches from his ship as the wounded Greeks are carried from the field. He sends Patroclus to learn who the wounded man in Nestor's chariot is—this moment begins the chain of events leading to Patroclus's death.

12.modern-en: Achilles remains absent as Hector and the Trojans break through the Greek wall.

13.modern-en: Achilles is still withdrawn as Poseidon secretly rallies the Greeks; his absence shapes the entire crisis.

14.modern-en: Achilles does not appear; the Greeks fight desperately without him.

15.modern-en: Achilles remains apart as Hector is healed by Apollo and drives the Greeks back to their very ships.

16.modern-en: Achilles relents enough to allow Patroclus to wear his armor and lead the Myrmidons into battle, warning him not to press too far. Patroclus dies at the hands of Euphorbus and Hector, and Achilles is consumed by grief when the news reaches him.

17.modern-en: Achilles does not yet know of Patroclus's death; the Greeks and Trojans fight desperately over the body.

18.modern-en: Achilles learns of Patroclus's death and collapses in grief. He swears vengeance on Hector. Thetis has Hephaestus forge him magnificent new armor, including the famous shield depicting the world.

19.modern-en: Achilles is reconciled with Agamemnon, gives up his anger, receives his armor, and re-enters the war—consumed entirely by the desire to kill Hector.

20.modern-en: Achilles returns to battle like a force of nature, cutting down Trojans on every side. Poseidon briefly saves Aeneas from his spear.

21.modern-en: Achilles slaughters Trojans so furiously that the river Scamander itself rises against him in anger; he takes twelve young Trojans prisoner to sacrifice at Patroclus's pyre.

22.modern-en: Achilles kills Hector before the walls of Troy, ties his body to his chariot, and drags it back to the Greek ships in savage grief and triumph.

23.modern-en: Achilles presides over Patroclus's elaborate funeral and the funeral games held in his honor, still raging with grief.

24.modern-en: Achilles is visited by old King Priam, who begs for Hector's body. Moved to pity, Achilles returns the body and grants a truce for Hector's funeral—a moment of hard-won humanity closing the poem.

epithet.en: King of Mycenae and commander-in-chief of the Greek forces, son of Atreus

1.modern-en: Agamemnon refuses to ransom the priest Chryses's daughter, causing Apollo's plague, then demands Achilles's captive Briseis as compensation—his arrogance ignites the central quarrel of the poem.

2.modern-en: Zeus sends Agamemnon a deceptive dream promising victory; he tests his troops by suggesting retreat but is nearly overwhelmed when they agree—Odysseus and Nestor restore order. Agamemnon then leads the great marshaling of forces.

3.modern-en: Agamemnon oversees the truce, administers oaths with Priam, and supports Menelaus's duel with Paris.

4.modern-en: After Pandarus wounds Menelaus and breaks the truce, Agamemnon rallies the army; he goes through the ranks encouraging and rebuking his captains.

5.modern-en: Agamemnon fights in the battle but is less prominent as Diomedes dominates the day.

6.modern-en: Agamemnon continues fighting in the general battle.

7.modern-en: Agamemnon supports the plan to build the Greek wall and ditch after the duel between Hector and Ajax.

8.modern-en: Zeus drives the Greeks back; Agamemnon laments and prays to Zeus as the Trojans push them to the wall.

9.modern-en: Agamemnon despairs and proposes retreat; he is talked down. He sends the embassy to Achilles with rich gifts and an apology—but Achilles refuses.

10.modern-en: Agamemnon cannot sleep, fearing disaster; he wakes Nestor and they organize the night watch and the spying mission.

11.modern-en: Agamemnon fights brilliantly at first, killing many Trojans, until he takes a spear wound in the arm and is forced to withdraw from battle.

12.modern-en: Agamemnon is absent from the front due to his wound as Hector breaks through the Greek wall.

13.modern-en: Agamemnon remains wounded as Poseidon secretly rallies the Greeks.

14.modern-en: Agamemnon proposes a humiliating retreat to the ships; Odysseus sharply rebukes him. Agamemnon eventually goes to fight despite his wound.

15.modern-en: Agamemnon fights in the desperate defense as Hector presses the Greeks back toward their ships.

16.modern-en: Agamemnon is among the wounded leaders whose plight moves Patroclus to beg Achilles for help.

17.modern-en: Agamemnon fights to defend Patroclus's body alongside the other Greeks.

18.modern-en: Agamemnon is mentioned as one of the wounded leaders still in camp.

19.modern-en: Agamemnon is formally reconciled with Achilles, publicly acknowledging that Zeus blinded his judgment; he gives Achilles the promised gifts including Briseis.

20.modern-en: Agamemnon returns to battle after the reconciliation.

21.modern-en: Agamemnon fights in the general battle as Achilles rampages through the Trojans.

22.modern-en: Agamemnon watches as Achilles kills Hector before the Trojan walls.

23.modern-en: Agamemnon participates in the funeral games for Patroclus.

24.modern-en: Agamemnon is present as the poem closes with Hector's burial, the war still unresolved.

epithet.en: Champion of Troy, eldest son of King Priam, husband of Andromache and father of Astyanax

1.modern-en: Hector is not yet prominent but is present in Troy as Achilles withdraws and the war's early tensions are established.

2.modern-en: Hector marshals the Trojan forces in the great catalogue of armies, leading them out to meet the Greeks.

3.modern-en: Hector rebukes his brother Paris for cowardice and arranges the single combat with Menelaus. He acts as intermediary between the armies.

4.modern-en: Hector leads the Trojans back into battle after Pandarus breaks the truce; he kills Eioneus in the fighting.

5.modern-en: Hector fights in the great battle but yields ground as Diomedes, empowered by Athena, rampages through the Trojan ranks.

6.modern-en: Hector returns to Troy to ask his mother to pray to Athena. He visits Paris and urges him back to battle. His farewell scene with Andromache and baby Astyanax is one of the poem's most tender and tragic moments.

7.modern-en: Hector challenges any Greek to single combat and fights Ajax to a draw; they exchange gifts as night falls. Hector oversees the Trojans' plan to return the dead and their proposal for a truce.

8.modern-en: Hector leads the Trojans to a great victory as Zeus favors them; he drives the Greeks back to their wall and the Trojans bivouac on the plain in triumph.

9.modern-en: Hector's success is so great that Agamemnon sends the embassy to Achilles; Hector is the threat that makes Achilles's return seem the only hope.

10.modern-en: Hector is on the plain with the Trojan forces as Odysseus and Diomedes carry out their night raid.

11.modern-en: Hector fights magnificently as Zeus gives the Trojans success; he wounds Diomedes and drives the Greeks back toward their ships.

12.modern-en: Hector leads the assault on the Greek wall and, seizing a great stone, smashes through the gates—a moment of supreme Trojan triumph.

13.modern-en: Hector fights at the Greek ships but is checked by Poseidon's intervention; he is blocked from breaking through entirely.

14.modern-en: Hector is struck with a boulder by Ajax and knocked unconscious; his Trojans carry him away from the fight.

15.modern-en: Apollo heals Hector and restores his strength; he leads a fierce assault that drives the Greeks to the very ships and nearly sets fire to the fleet.

16.modern-en: Hector kills Patroclus—the pivotal event of the Iliad—stripping him of Achilles's armor after Euphorbus first wounded him.

17.modern-en: Hector fights over Patroclus's body, donning Achilles's own armor; he is checked by the Greeks led by Menelaus and Ajax.

18.modern-en: Hector rejects the wise counsel of Polydamas to retreat inside Troy's walls, choosing to meet Achilles in battle—a fatal decision driven by pride.

19.modern-en: Hector does not appear directly; Achilles prepares for battle with the sole aim of killing him.

20.modern-en: Hector is warned by Apollo to avoid Achilles; he stays back as Achilles cuts down other Trojans.

21.modern-en: Hector retreats inside Troy's walls as Achilles rampages; Apollo tricks Achilles to delay the final confrontation.

22.modern-en: Hector waits outside the walls alone; loses his nerve and flees three times around the city before Athena tricks him into standing firm. Achilles kills him. As he dies, Hector asks that his body be returned to his family—Achilles refuses.

23.modern-en: Hector's body is dragged behind Achilles's chariot around Patroclus's funeral pyre; the gods protect it from decay.

24.modern-en: Hector's body is ransomed by Priam and returned to Troy. The poem ends with his funeral—twelve days of lamentation, cremation, and burial.

epithet.en: Achilles's closest companion and comrade, son of Menoetius

1.modern-en: Patroclus is present but not yet prominent, serving as Achilles's companion at the ships.

9.modern-en: Patroclus is present during the embassy and is mentioned as a witness; he will later carry out Achilles's instructions.

11.modern-en: Achilles sends Patroclus to inquire who Nestor is bringing wounded from the field. Nestor makes a long speech urging Patroclus to persuade Achilles to return, or at least let Patroclus wear his armor—the seed of the tragedy is planted.

15.modern-en: Patroclus tends to the wounded Eurypylus in his tent as the battle rages; his compassion for suffering Greeks increases his resolve to act.

16.modern-en: Patroclus weeps before Achilles, begging to enter the battle wearing Achilles's armor. Achilles relents but warns him not to press too far. Patroclus drives the Trojans back brilliantly but ignores Achilles's warning; wounded by Euphorbus and then killed by Hector, he dies warning Hector that Achilles will avenge him.

17.modern-en: Greeks and Trojans fight savagely over Patroclus's naked body; the Greeks eventually recover it, though Hector keeps Achilles's armor.

18.modern-en: Achilles receives the news of Patroclus's death and is devastated; his grief transforms his wrath from sullen anger to grief-driven fury for vengeance.

19.modern-en: Achilles prepares Patroclus's body for burial and swears over it that Hector will die.

23.modern-en: Patroclus's ghost appears to Achilles asking for burial; his elaborate funeral includes a great pyre, human sacrifices, and funeral games in his honor.

24.modern-en: Patroclus's memory drives Achilles even after Hector's death; his tomb is where Achilles drags Hector's body.

epithet.en: King of Sparta and husband of Helen, whose abduction by Paris started the war

1.modern-en: Menelaus is present but not central; the quarrel between Achilles and Agamemnon overshadows his cause.

3.modern-en: Menelaus duels Paris in single combat to settle the war; he has nearly won when Aphrodite spirits Paris away. Menelaus searches furiously among the Trojans for his vanished opponent.

4.modern-en: Pandarus wounds Menelaus with an arrow, breaking the truce. Agamemnon tends anxiously to the wound; it proves minor. Menelaus fights in the ensuing battle.

7.modern-en: Menelaus wants to fight Hector in single combat but is wisely restrained by Agamemnon and the other Greeks who fear he would lose.

10.modern-en: Menelaus cannot sleep and wakes Agamemnon; he participates in organizing the night watch.

13.modern-en: Menelaus fights bravely in the defense, killing Hyperenor and other Trojans.

17.modern-en: Menelaus stands over Patroclus's body like a cow over her calf, defending it fiercely. He kills Euphorbus, who had first wounded Patroclus. He and Ajax work together to carry the body to safety.

22.modern-en: Menelaus watches as Achilles kills Hector.

23.modern-en: Menelaus competes in the funeral games for Patroclus, notably in the chariot race where he is nearly cheated by Antilochus.

24.modern-en: Menelaus is present as the poem closes with Hector's burial, still awaiting the return of Helen.

epithet.en: Shrewd and resourceful king of Ithaca, the Greeks' greatest counselor and tactician

2.modern-en: When Agamemnon's test speech triggers a near-stampede to the ships, Odysseus seizes the scepter and restores order, rallying the Greeks with hard words and blows.

3.modern-en: Helen describes Odysseus to Priam from the wall—shorter than Agamemnon but more regal when seated, and a devastating orator.

4.modern-en: Agamemnon briefly reproaches Odysseus for standing back; Odysseus retorts sharply, and Agamemnon quickly withdraws his words.

9.modern-en: Odysseus leads the embassy to Achilles, delivering the offer of gifts with skilled diplomacy. Achilles rejects him, but Odysseus reports honestly to the Greeks.

10.modern-en: Odysseus and Diomedes carry out the night raid, capturing and killing the Trojan spy Dolon, then killing the sleeping Thracian king Rhesus and driving off his famous horses.

11.modern-en: Odysseus is wounded in the fighting but continues to fight; he kills several Trojans before withdrawing with a spear wound.

14.modern-en: Odysseus sharply rebukes Agamemnon's proposal to flee, reminding him of what such cowardice would mean for the army.

19.modern-en: Odysseus urges the army to eat before battle, arguing that men cannot fight on empty stomachs.

23.modern-en: Odysseus competes in the funeral games, winning the wrestling match against Ajax and showing characteristic cleverness in the footrace.

epithet.en: Towering son of Telamon, the Greeks' greatest warrior after Achilles, known for his massive shield and stubborn courage

2.modern-en: Ajax is listed in the catalogue of ships, leading the contingent from Salamis with twelve ships.

3.modern-en: Helen points Ajax out to Priam from the walls of Troy—'huge Ajax, bulwark of the Achaeans.'

4.modern-en: Ajax kills Simoeisius early in the battle, one of several notable kills as fighting begins in earnest.

6.modern-en: Ajax kills Acamas, continuing to fight fiercely in the general battle.

7.modern-en: Ajax is chosen by lot to fight Hector in single combat. The duel ends at nightfall with neither man victorious; they exchange gifts as a mark of respect.

8.modern-en: Ajax fights in the retreat, covering the Greeks as they fall back toward their wall.

11.modern-en: Ajax fights bravely as the Greeks are pushed back; he and his namesake (Ajax the Lesser) form a fighting rearguard.

12.modern-en: Ajax and Teucer defend the wall from the battlements, shooting arrows and hurling stones at the Trojans.

13.modern-en: Ajax fights fiercely in the defense, killing Trojans who try to force through to the ships.

14.modern-en: Ajax strikes Hector with a great boulder, knocking him senseless—temporarily turning the tide.

15.modern-en: Ajax fights with extraordinary valor defending the ships with a long boarding pike, killing many Trojans.

16.modern-en: Ajax fights to recover Patroclus's body after he is killed.

17.modern-en: Ajax and Menelaus work together to defend and then carry off Patroclus's body from the Trojans.

23.modern-en: Ajax competes in the funeral games; he and Odysseus draw in the wrestling match, and he loses the footrace narrowly.

epithet.en: Bold young king of Argos, son of Tydeus, whose aristeia (day of glory) fills Book V

4.modern-en: Agamemnon reproaches Diomedes for hanging back; Diomedes accepts the rebuke quietly, showing discipline over pride.

5.modern-en: Athena empowers Diomedes to his greatest day—he kills Pandarus, wounds Aeneas, and then, uniquely among mortals, wounds both Aphrodite and Ares on the battlefield.

6.modern-en: Diomedes meets the Lycian Glaucus; they discover their families are guest-friends and exchange armor rather than fight.

9.modern-en: Diomedes speaks at the assembly, arguing that no gifts should be offered to Achilles—his pride must be left to work itself out.

10.modern-en: Diomedes and Odysseus carry out the night raid, killing the spy Dolon, slaying Rhesus the Thracian king, and stealing his famous white horses.

11.modern-en: Diomedes fights well but is wounded in the foot by Paris's arrow and forced to withdraw from battle.

14.modern-en: Although wounded, Diomedes rejoins the fighting at the urging of Odysseus and the others.

23.modern-en: Diomedes wins the chariot race in the funeral games for Patroclus.

epithet.en: Elderly king of Pylos, the Greeks' wisest counselor, renowned for long speeches full of tales from his heroic youth

1.modern-en: Nestor intervenes in the quarrel between Achilles and Agamemnon, urging both to yield—neither fully listens, but he establishes himself as the voice of wisdom.

2.modern-en: Nestor speaks in the assembly after Odysseus restores order, supporting the plan to fight and marshal the troops.

4.modern-en: Agamemnon praises Nestor's wisdom and laments that age has weakened him; Nestor marshals his troops skillfully, placing cavalry in front.

7.modern-en: Nestor proposes that the Greeks build a wall and ditch around their ships after the duel between Hector and Ajax.

9.modern-en: Nestor organizes the embassy to Achilles and selects its members.

10.modern-en: Nestor cannot sleep; he and Agamemnon organize the night watch and authorize the spying mission.

11.modern-en: Nestor drives the wounded Machaon back to camp in his chariot. When Patroclus comes to ask who was wounded, Nestor delivers a long speech recounting his youthful exploits, urging Patroclus to persuade Achilles—or at least to borrow his armor.

14.modern-en: Nestor notices the battle's roar and goes to the wall; he sees the rout and joins the council that rejects Agamemnon's plan to flee.

23.modern-en: Nestor gives his son Antilochus tactical advice before the chariot race; his wisdom proves useful even here.

epithet.en: Aged king of Troy, father of Hector and Paris, who endures the war's devastation with dignity

3.modern-en: Priam watches the armies from the walls of Troy, asking Helen to identify the Greek leaders. He joins the truce ceremony on the plain to swear oaths, then returns to the city rather than watch his son Paris fight.

6.modern-en: Priam does not appear directly but is mentioned by Hector as he goes to check on the royal house.

7.modern-en: Priam and the Trojans discuss the Greek offer of a truce to bury the dead; they agree to return the bodies but not Helen.

22.modern-en: Priam watches in agony from the walls as Achilles kills Hector and drags his body away. He is forcibly restrained from rushing out; his grief is overwhelming.

24.modern-en: Priam makes an extraordinary journey alone to the Greek camp, guided by Hermes. He kneels before Achilles and begs for Hector's body, kissing the hands that killed his son. Achilles is moved to tears; the body is returned and Priam leads the funeral rites.

epithet.en: Trojan prince whose abduction of Helen caused the war; handsome but unreliable in battle, also called Alexandrus

3.modern-en: Paris challenges the Greeks to single combat but shrinks in fear when Menelaus steps forward. He duels Menelaus and is losing badly when Aphrodite spirits him away to his bedroom; he reappears with no shame, trying to seduce Helen.

4.modern-en: Pandarus shoots at Menelaus partly out of hope that Alexandrus would reward him.

6.modern-en: Hector visits Paris and urges him back to battle; Paris is found with Helen, reluctant to fight, but eventually arms and follows Hector to the field.

7.modern-en: Paris speaks in the Trojan assembly, offering to return Helen's treasure but refusing to give back Helen herself.

11.modern-en: Paris wounds Diomedes in the foot with an arrow and wounds Machaon—both significant blows, showing that Paris, though no hand-to-hand fighter, is effective as an archer.

13.modern-en: Paris fights with his bow in the defense of Troy.

24.modern-en: Paris is mentioned briefly as the cause of the whole war; the gods remember his judgment on Olympus as the reason Hera and Athena hate Troy.

epithet.en: Hector's devoted wife and mother of Astyanax, who foresees Troy's doom with heartbreaking clarity

6.modern-en: Andromache meets Hector at the Scaean gates in the poem's most tender scene. She begs him not to fight, reminding him that Achilles killed her father and brothers, making Hector her only family. Hector takes off his helmet to kiss their baby Astyanax, who is frightened by the crest. He acknowledges the doom ahead but refuses to hide from his duty.

22.modern-en: Andromache hears the wailing from the walls and rushes to see Hector's body being dragged behind Achilles's chariot. Her lament is devastating—she mourns not just his death but Astyanax's fatherless future.

24.modern-en: Andromache leads the women in mourning at Hector's funeral, lamenting both the man she has lost and the city she knows will soon fall.

epithet.en: The most beautiful woman in the world, whose abduction from Sparta by Paris brought the Greek fleet to Troy

3.modern-en: Helen stands on the walls of Troy identifying Greek leaders for Priam. She laments her own role in causing the war with evident guilt. After Aphrodite spirits Paris away, the goddess forces Helen to return to his bedroom against her will; Helen reproaches Paris bitterly.

6.modern-en: Helen speaks with Hector when he visits Paris; she regrets her situation and mourns that she was not married to a better man. Hector treats her kindly.

24.modern-en: Helen delivers one of the last laments over Hector's body, saying he was always kind to her when others in Troy were not—the only one who truly treated her with compassion.

epithet.en: Queen of Troy and wife of Priam, mother of Hector and Paris, who mourns the unfolding destruction

6.modern-en: Hector asks his mother Hecuba to lead the Trojan women in prayer to Athena, offering a robe at her temple in hopes the goddess will have mercy on Troy.

22.modern-en: Hecuba cries out in anguish from the walls as she watches Achilles kill Hector; she tears her robes and weeps.

24.modern-en: Hecuba tries to dissuade Priam from his dangerous mission to Achilles, fearing he will be killed. After Priam brings back Hector's body, she leads the women in lamentation.

epithet.en: Trojan prince and cousin of Hector, son of Aphrodite and Anchises, destined to survive and found a new people

5.modern-en: Aeneas is nearly killed by Diomedes, who wounds him with a boulder; Aphrodite rescues him but is herself wounded when she carries him off. Apollo then takes Aeneas away to be healed before returning him to battle.

13.modern-en: Aeneas fights bravely in the defense against the Greeks and is encouraged by Poseidon (secretly favoring him for future greatness).

17.modern-en: Aeneas fights in the battle over Patroclus's body.

20.modern-en: Aeneas is urged by Apollo to meet Achilles directly; a remarkable duel is interrupted by Poseidon, who envelops Aeneas in mist and carries him to safety—because Aeneas is fated to survive and continue his lineage.

epithet.en: King of Lycia and son of Zeus, the greatest of Troy's allies, killed by Patroclus in Book XVI

5.modern-en: Sarpedon fights bravely and is wounded by Tlepolemus, whom he kills; he is carried from the field by his Lycian comrades.

12.modern-en: Sarpedon leads the attack on the Greek wall with stirring words to his companion Glaucus about the duty of leaders who enjoy great honor to fight at the front.

16.modern-en: Sarpedon is killed by Patroclus—Zeus laments his son's death but is persuaded by Hera not to intervene. His body is carried off the battlefield by Sleep and Death on Zeus's orders, to be buried in Lycia with honors.

epithet.en: Old tutor and foster-father of Achilles, who accompanies the embassy to plead for his return

9.modern-en: Phoenix is sent with Odysseus and Ajax to Achilles. He delivers a deeply personal speech, recalling how he raised Achilles from infancy and telling the story of Meleager to argue that even great heroes must relent. Achilles is moved but still refuses to return to battle immediately.

17.modern-en: Phoenix is mentioned among those who weep over Patroclus.

19.modern-en: Phoenix is present as Achilles arms for his return to battle.

23.modern-en: Phoenix participates in the funeral rites and games for Patroclus.

epithet.en: Captive woman taken by Achilles from Lyrnessus, whose seizure by Agamemnon ignites Achilles's wrath

1.modern-en: Agamemnon demands Briseis as compensation for returning Chryseis; Achilles yields her only under protest, and her seizure is the act that drives Achilles from the war.

9.modern-en: Briseis is central to the embassy's offer—Agamemnon promises to return her, untouched, as part of his apology gifts to Achilles.

19.modern-en: Briseis is formally returned to Achilles at the reconciliation. She weeps over Patroclus's body, lamenting that he had always been kind to her and had promised she would become Achilles's wife.

epithet.en: Daughter of the priest Chryses, whose captivity causes Apollo's plague and sets the whole story in motion

1.modern-en: Chryseis is the captive of Agamemnon; her father Chryses comes to ransom her but is rudely turned away. Apollo sends a plague on the Greeks. Chryseis is ultimately returned to her father, ending the plague but starting the quarrel over Briseis.

epithet.en: Sea-goddess and mother of Achilles, who intercedes with Zeus on her son's behalf and has his divine armor forged

1.modern-en: Thetis hears Achilles's grief and appeals to Zeus to honor her son by giving the Trojans victory until the Greeks beg Achilles to return.

18.modern-en: Thetis comes to comfort Achilles after Patroclus's death and visits Hephaestus to commission magnificent new armor for her son, including the famous divine shield.

19.modern-en: Thetis brings the new armor to Achilles and promises to preserve Patroclus's body from decay while Achilles goes to fight.

24.modern-en: Zeus sends Thetis to tell Achilles he must return Hector's body; she carries the message and Achilles obeys.

epithet.en: King of the gods and father of gods and men, whose will shapes the outcome of the war

1.modern-en: Zeus agrees to Thetis's request to honor Achilles by giving the Trojans victory, setting the tragic machinery of the poem in motion.

2.modern-en: Zeus sends a deceptive dream to Agamemnon promising victory—a false promise that delays rather than delivers triumph.

4.modern-en: Zeus sits in council on Olympus as Hera and Athena plot; he permits Athena to have Pandarus break the truce.

8.modern-en: Zeus forbids the gods from interfering and tips his golden scales to favor the Trojans, driving the Greeks back to their wall.

11.modern-en: Zeus gives the Trojans victory through most of the day, fulfilling his promise to Thetis.

14.modern-en: Hera seduces Zeus and puts him to sleep so Poseidon can help the Greeks; Zeus wakes furious but too late.

15.modern-en: Zeus wakes and angrily reverses the battle's course, sending Apollo to heal Hector and drive the Greeks back.

16.modern-en: Zeus watches as Sarpedon, his son, is killed by Patroclus—Hera dissuades him from intervening, and Zeus weeps tears of blood.

20.modern-en: Zeus allows the gods to join the fighting freely for the first time, taking sides.

22.modern-en: Zeus tips his golden scales and Hector's fate sinks—the gods must allow Achilles to kill him despite Zeus's affection for the Trojan.

24.modern-en: Zeus takes pity on Hector's corpse being dishonored and sends Thetis to tell Achilles to return the body; he arranges Priam's safe passage to the Greek camp.

epithet.en: Queen of the gods and fierce champion of the Greeks, who schemes relentlessly against Troy

1.modern-en: Hera argues with Zeus on Olympus after Thetis's visit; she is suspicious that he is favoring the Trojans.

4.modern-en: Hera and Athena sit in Olympus muttering against Zeus's plan for peace; Hera pushes Athena to go break the truce.

8.modern-en: Hera and Athena set out to help the Greeks but are turned back by Zeus's messenger Iris with a sharp warning from Zeus.

14.modern-en: Hera famously seduces Zeus, borrowing Aphrodite's enchanted girdle to put him to sleep so Poseidon can secretly help the Greeks—one of the poem's great comic-divine episodes.

15.modern-en: Zeus wakes, discovers Hera's deception, and angrily forces her to recall the gods aiding the Greeks.

18.modern-en: Hera is among those gods who insist Hector's body must be returned; she holds firm against Trojans throughout.

24.modern-en: Hera is one of the gods who resists the idea of returning Hector's body; she hates Troy too deeply for that, though Zeus overrules her.

epithet.en: Goddess of wisdom and war, the Greeks' most active divine champion, who intervenes repeatedly and decisively

1.modern-en: Athena appears to Achilles when he is about to draw his sword on Agamemnon, holding him back; she promises him rich gifts if he restrains himself.

4.modern-en: Athena disguises herself as a Trojan ally and persuades the archer Pandarus to shoot at Menelaus, breaking the truce.

5.modern-en: Athena is Diomedes's patron through his entire aristeia—she gives him the power to see gods, guides his spear, and holds Ares back; when Diomedes wounds Ares she rejoices.

7.modern-en: Athena and Apollo together arrange the single combat between Hector and Ajax to pause the day's fighting.

8.modern-en: Athena is called back from helping the Greeks by Zeus's orders; she and Hera obey, furious.

10.modern-en: Athena guides Odysseus and Diomedes on their night raid, helping them find and kill Rhesus.

15.modern-en: Athena is restrained by Zeus's command from openly helping the Greeks.

17.modern-en: Athena comes down disguised to rally Menelaus and the Greeks in their fight for Patroclus's body.

20.modern-en: Athena joins the battle on the Greek side as Zeus allows the gods to fight; she opposes Ares directly.

22.modern-en: Athena tricks Hector into standing his ground by disguising herself as his brother Deiphobus; when Hector realizes the deception after his spear misses Achilles, he knows his death is certain.

epithet.en: God of the sun and archery, Troy's greatest divine protector, who supports Hector and the Trojans throughout

1.modern-en: Apollo sends a devastating plague on the Greek camp when his priest Chryses is insulted by Agamemnon; the plague forces the Greeks to return Chryseis and starts the whole chain of events.

4.modern-en: Apollo calls out encouragement to the Trojans during the battle, reminding them that Achilles is not fighting.

5.modern-en: Apollo rescues Aeneas from Diomedes, covering him with a cloud and carrying him away; he repeatedly confronts Diomedes, who finally backs down from fighting a god directly.

7.modern-en: Apollo collaborates with Athena to arrange the single combat and pause the day's battle.

15.modern-en: Zeus sends Apollo to heal Hector and reinvigorate the Trojan assault; Apollo effectively demolishes the Greek wall and drives the Greeks back to their ships.

16.modern-en: Apollo strips the armor from Patroclus and stuns him before Euphorbus and then Hector deliver their blows—the god's intervention seals Patroclus's fate.

19.modern-en: Apollo protects Hector's body through much of the battle.

20.modern-en: Apollo urges Aeneas to confront Achilles; he supports the Trojans as the gods enter the battle.

21.modern-en: Apollo delays Achilles by disguising himself as a Trojan warrior and leading him on a chase, buying time for the Trojans to escape inside their walls.

22.modern-en: Apollo abandons Hector at the moment of his fatal encounter with Achilles, acknowledging that fate demands Hector die.

24.modern-en: Apollo protects Hector's body from decay and dishonor as Achilles drags it around the camp; he argues for its return in the divine council.

epithet.en: God of the sea, the Greeks' secret ally, who intervenes to save them from defeat despite Zeus's prohibition

7.modern-en: Poseidon watches the Greeks build their wall from the sea; he and Zeus discuss whether it threatens the gods' honor.

12.modern-en: Poseidon watches Hector's triumph with anger; he disagrees with Zeus's pro-Trojan policy but is bound to obey.

13.modern-en: Poseidon secretly descends to rally the Greeks while Zeus looks away, assuming the form of Calchas and inspiring the two Ajaxes and Idomeneus.

14.modern-en: Poseidon openly leads the Greek counterattack while Zeus sleeps, thanks to Hera's deception.

15.modern-en: Zeus wakes and forces Poseidon to withdraw his help from the Greeks.

20.modern-en: Zeus allows Poseidon to fight on the Greek side; Poseidon saves Aeneas from Achilles, carrying him to safety.

21.modern-en: Poseidon and Athena oppose Ares and other Trojan-supporting gods in the divine battle.

epithet.en: Goddess of love, Troy's partisan deity, who protects Paris and is memorably wounded by Diomedes

3.modern-en: Aphrodite saves Paris from Menelaus by breaking his chinstrap and whisking him off to his bedroom; she then compels a reluctant Helen to go to him.

5.modern-en: Aphrodite rescues the wounded Aeneas but is herself wounded on the wrist by Diomedes—the first time a mortal has injured a god. She flees to Olympus weeping; Dione her mother comforts her and Zeus gently rebukes her for meddling in war.

14.modern-en: Hera borrows Aphrodite's enchanted girdle of desire to seduce Zeus—an ironic use of love's power for strategic ends.

20.modern-en: Aphrodite fights on the Trojan side as the gods enter open battle.

21.modern-en: Athena knocks Aphrodite down when she helps the wounded Ares off the battlefield.

epithet.en: God of war, who sides with Troy and is twice humiliated—wounded by Diomedes in Book V and knocked down by Athena in Book XXI

5.modern-en: Ares fights fiercely for the Trojans until Diomedes, guided by Athena, wounds him with a spear; Ares screams like ten thousand men and flees to Olympus, where Zeus reprimands him.

15.modern-en: Ares learns that his son Ascalaphus has been killed and prepares to join the battle in grief and rage, but Athena restrains him.

20.modern-en: Ares joins the battle on the Trojan side as Zeus allows the gods to fight openly.

21.modern-en: Ares is knocked to the ground by Athena in the divine battle; Aphrodite helps him away.

epithet.en: Divine smith and craftsman, who forges Achilles's magnificent new armor at Thetis's request

1.modern-en: Hephaestus intervenes in the quarrel between Zeus and Hera, urging his mother to yield; he pours nectar for the gods, earning laughter and defusing the tension.

18.modern-en: Thetis visits Hephaestus in his forge; his grateful wife Charis greets her warmly. He crafts Achilles's new armor over the course of the night, most famously the great shield depicting the whole of human life.

20.modern-en: Hephaestus fights on the Greek side, opposing the river Scamander with fire when the river threatens to drown Achilles.

21.modern-en: Hephaestus fights the flooded river Xanthus with fire at Hera's request, drying up its banks and forcing the river to relent.

epithet.en: Messenger god and guide of souls, who escorts Priam safely through the Greek camp to Achilles

24.modern-en: Zeus sends Hermes to guide old Priam through the Greek camp at night. Hermes disguises himself as a young Greek nobleman and escorts Priam's wagon directly to Achilles's tent, then departs before dawn.

epithet.en: Swift captain of the Locrians, son of Oileus, a formidable warrior though morally inferior to his great namesake

2.modern-en: Ajax the Lesser is listed in the catalogue of ships, leading the Locrians.

13.modern-en: Ajax the Lesser fights in the defense of the ships alongside his greater namesake.

14.modern-en: The two Ajaxes fight together in the Greek rally after Hector is wounded.

23.modern-en: Ajax the Lesser competes in the footrace at the funeral games but slips in cattle dung just before the finish, losing narrowly to Odysseus.

epithet.en: Veteran king of Crete, a trusted ally of Agamemnon who fights brilliantly in his own aristeia in Books XIII–XIV

3.modern-en: Helen identifies Idomeneus to Priam from the walls; he stands out among the Cretan contingent.

4.modern-en: Agamemnon praises Idomeneus and gives him a cup always kept full—a mark of special favor.

13.modern-en: Idomeneus has his aristeia—a major stretch of fighting glory. He kills many Trojans including Alcathous and fights Aeneas to a standstill.

17.modern-en: Idomeneus fights in the battle over Patroclus's body.

23.modern-en: Idomeneus and Ajax the Lesser argue over the chariot race results, requiring Achilles to adjudicate.

epithet.en: Lycian captain and close friend of Sarpedon, whose exchange of armor with Diomedes is one of the poem's famous episodes

6.modern-en: Glaucus meets Diomedes on the battlefield; when they discover their grandfathers were guest-friends, they exchange armor as a sign of the old bond—Glaucus gives gold armor worth one hundred oxen in exchange for bronze worth nine.

12.modern-en: Sarpedon gives his famous speech on the duty of heroes to Glaucus before their attack on the Greek wall.

16.modern-en: Glaucus is wounded and prays to Apollo, who heals him so he can return to defend Sarpedon's body.

17.modern-en: Glaucus rebukes Hector for not fighting for Sarpedon's body; Hector puts on Achilles's captured armor.
